deep_why: The core insight is identifying and fixing a systematic bias in how models focus on sequence positions. When attention mechanisms concentrate disproportionately on the start and end of a sequence while ignoring the middle, the model misses crucial behavioral information. The method works because masking unreliable position-based attention signals during training removes the architectural pattern that favors boundaries. By then applying counterfactual adjustments at test time—asking what the prediction would be without position cues—the system can measure and subtract away the residual position-only effects. This two-stage approach (training-time removal plus inference-time correction) guarantees the model learns meaningful patterns from actual behavior rather than relying on positional shortcuts, ensuring recommendations reflect true user interests rather than spurious boundary signals.

Person retrieval from text descriptions must capture fine-grained identity details—skin tone, clothing, pose—while learning from limited adapted capacity and noisy image-text pairs. The method works by using a multi-level adapter that decouples global appearance from local spatial details, letting each level specialize. Simultaneously, the reliability-aware reweighting downweights mislabeled pairs during training, so the model learns primarily from clean examples. This combination ensures the adapted model genuinely learns identity cues rather than spurious correlations in noisy data. The cyclic verification step—checking that retrieved results have consistent cross-modal agreement—provides a final consistency filter that catches retrieval errors. Together, these layers prevent overfitting on misleading signal, letting the limited adaptation capacity focus on real identifying features that generalize to new domains.

User interests naturally span popular trends and obscure niche preferences, but standard message-passing treats them uniformly. The key principle is that popular and niche items live in different frequency bands of the user-item graph signal: popular items have consistent, repeating patterns across many users, while niche items show rare, idiosyncratic patterns. Decomposing the graph signal by frequency separates these two regimes mathematically. Once separated, the model can apply adaptive fusion strategies tailored to each type—strong signal aggregation for popular items and careful preservation of sparse niche cues. This separation guarantees the model captures both types of interest without the dominant popular signal drowning out rare preferences, solving the core recommendation challenge of delivering both familiar-and-good and surprising-and-personal results.

Table retrieval fails when the text representation loses structural information that disambiguates meaning—for instance, the same word in different table cells has different semantics depending on column context. The core principle is that tabular structure is a built-in consistency constraint: entities aligned in the same column share semantic type, and linked knowledge graphs provide external validation. By modeling the table corpus directly rather than learning from query examples, the system can discover what patterns genuinely distinguish one table from another. Combining dense semantic matching with symbolic graph-based verification and sparse lexical anchors creates multiple independent pathways that must agree, so spurious matches fail the consistency check. This multi-modal reasoning grounds query interpretation in the structure itself rather than memorized query patterns, ensuring retrieval generalizes to completely new queries with no training examples.

Legal retrieval needs both broad recall and high precision, but running separate retriever and reranker models causes errors to compound—a missed document in stage one can never be recovered. Sharing parameters in one unified model eliminates this error propagation because retrieval and reranking decisions come from the same learned representations. The Phantom Hits problem—irrelevant documents scored high—occurs when the model sees isolated relevant words without grasping context. The solution is to train explicitly on pure-negative groups (candidates with zero relevance signals) and use margin-based ranking that forces the model to score irrelevant documents consistently low even when they contain some matching keywords. Adding maximum entropy regularization prevents the model from overconfidently assigning high scores to ambiguous cases. These mechanisms combined ensure irrelevant documents stay confidently ranked low, letting high precision and broad recall coexist within one architecture.

Graph recommendation models learn to quantize—represent in low-bit format—to run on edge devices, but naively quantizing all embeddings equally wastes bits because node embeddings have heterogeneous structure: some dimensions vary smoothly while others cluster. The method works by adaptively partitioning node embeddings into chunks based on their value distributions. Nodes with similar embedding patterns get the same quantization scheme, so the model preserves crucial distinctions (like separating popular items from niche ones) while aggressively compressing redundant information. In quantization-aware training, these chunk boundaries adapt dynamically as the model learns, so compression targets the least informative dimensions. In post-training mode, clustering nodes first ensures nodes with coherent meaning share quantization settings. This adaptive, distribution-aware approach guarantees high-accuracy low-bitwidth models because it compresses waste and preserves signal, not the reverse.

Retrieving 3D models from 2D images is hard because images and 3D shapes come from different domains with different class boundaries—a chair photographed upside-down might classify one way in images but differently in 3D. The core principle is that good retrieval requires both matching decision boundaries and preserving neighborhood structure. Aligning class boundaries via adversarial min-max optimization forces the 2D and 3D classifiers to agree on what separates similar categories, eliminating spurious domain-specific definitions. Complementing this with graph semantic propagation ensures that if two 3D shapes are neighbors in feature space, their 2D counterparts remain neighbors too, preserving the intrinsic structure. Constructing balanced mini-batches by category prevents popular classes from drowning out rare ones during learning. Together, boundary alignment plus neighborhood preservation guarantee the system learns genuine cross-modal similarity that transfers to retrieval rather than exploiting domain-specific shortcuts.

Depression detection from social media requires integrating visual and acoustic cues that carry different signals—facial expression changes over video frames while tone-of-voice conveys emotional state. The method uses mutual guidance to automatically identify what visual patterns help interpret audio signals and vice versa. Building a complementary graph capturing these cross-modal associations lets the model weight each modality appropriately for each sample—sometimes audio is more informative, sometimes visual cues dominate. Applying adaptive residual learning to each modality preserves its unique strength while integrating shared signals. This approach works because it respects the fundamental truth that depression manifests differently across modalities: direct correlation might miss depression when someone maintains composed facial expression despite vocal distress. By letting each modality maintain its identity while being guided by the other, the model avoids averaging away genuine cross-modal disagreements that carry diagnostic signal.

User preferences contain both long-term trends and short-term impulses, but they operate on different time scales and noise characteristics: short-term actions are noisy but reactive, while long-term preferences are stable but slow-moving. The method decomposes the frequency spectrum to separate these regimes—high frequencies capture the noisy short-term variations while low frequencies hold the clean long-term signal. The core principle is energy-aware denoising: instead of uniformly suppressing noise, the model adaptively dampens low-energy noise in each band while preserving high-energy behavior signals. Using separate decoupled branches for each frequency band lets each branch specialize in the temporal patterns it sees. Dynamically gating how much to weight each branch ensures the final recommendation balances quick reactions to recent behavior with stable respect for fundamental preferences. This separation guarantees recommendations respond flexibly to context without being derailed by momentary random clicks.

Editing knowledge in large multimodal models is dangerous because changing one fact can ripple through the entire network, corrupting other knowledge. The method works by treating editing as a neuron-level intervention rather than global changes. First, it identifies exactly which neurons fire when the model retrieves a specific fact—the neurons that causally determine the answer. This localization is sound because neurons represent coherent concepts, so isolating the responsible subset prevents collateral damage. Second, it injects context-aware updates into only those neurons, allowing them to use context clues to decide whether to retrieve the old knowledge or newly supplied corrected information. This approach guarantees edits stay localized because irrelevant neurons are untouched, and the edited neurons can recover default behavior when context indicates the old knowledge should still apply. Controlling exactly where and how to intervene prevents the false certainty that ruins knowledge editing.

Entity linking must resolve which person, place, or thing a mention refers to, using information from text, images, and knowledge bases that often disagree or contradict. The core challenge is that some elements—like image or text—can dominate the decision, causing the model to miss crucial signals. The method uses a divide-and-conquer strategy: separate experts handle different element types (text tokens, visual regions, knowledge structure) so each can contribute without being suppressed. A routing mechanism ensures expert specialization—text expert learns text patterns, visual expert learns visual patterns. A hierarchical multimodal interaction module dynamically weights how much each expert should influence the final decision, and this weighting adapts at multiple semantic levels. This multi-level approach works because entity linking succeeds when all available signals agree: decision boundaries confirmed at fine-grained levels, and neighborhood structure preserved at coarse levels. By preventing dominance and building consensus across levels, the system leverages complementary evidence rather than betting on one modality.

Complex search queries require reasoning about multiple subtasks—finding background knowledge, synthesizing information, planning next steps—but most models handle planning and execution in one pass, causing execution details to disrupt high-level strategy. The method decouples them: a planning layer decomposes the query into subtasks, routing each to a specialized agent with domain-specific tools and knowledge. This separation is sound because different reasoning types work best on different abstractions—planning needs a clean bird's-eye view while execution needs contextual detail. Each specialized agent can optimize for its specific problem (finding tables, conducting numerical reasoning, or conversational synthesis). Coordinating results through a structured integration mechanism ensures the final answer respects both the overall plan and the specialized outputs. This hierarchical architecture guarantees complex reasoning succeeds because planning doesn't get tangled in execution minutiae, and execution can focus deeply without worrying about global coherence.

Table retrieval instructions demand more than topical similarity: they specify content constraints like include-this-column-exclude-that-row and schema requirements like find-numeric-aggregations. Traditional relevance scoring ignores these because it only matches topics. The method works by treating instructions as explicit constraints that must be satisfied alongside relevance. Building a benchmark where instructions genuinely require different tables forces the model to learn to distinguish topically similar tables by their structural properties. The Instruction Responsiveness Score measures whether ranking changes appropriately when instructions change, directly testing instruction-sensitivity rather than just overall relevance. This metric-driven approach ensures models learn that instructions override topic similarity when they conflict. The core principle is that consistent instruction-following requires both understanding language constraints and knowing schema semantics—column types, value domains, granularity levels. By explicitly measuring these abilities, the method guarantees models develop instruction awareness rather than defaulting to topic matching.

Collaborative filtering learns user preferences from past interactions, but naive contrastive learning forces different users apart even when they genuinely like the same items, creating false negatives. The core insight is that user separation should happen at the right level of representation. The method applies contrastive regularization to hidden encoder representations rather than final prediction scores. This separation is sound because encoder representations capture preference structure while avoiding the output-level problem where same-preference users would be penalized for similarity. Flow matching is sensitive to input perturbations, so traditional view construction—adding noise to create training pairs—causes mismatches where the two views should be positively paired but flow matching generates different outputs. By keeping the input fixed and only applying contrastive constraints to the encoder representation, the method avoids this mismatch. This hidden-level approach guarantees the model learns user-specific preference patterns because separation happens in representation space where similarity meaningfully reflects preference alignment, not arbitrary output differences.

MCP servers offer functionality through tools with unclear or scattered documentation, making it hard for LLM agents to find the right server for a task. The method works by extracting precise function inventory from server code—what each tool actually does, what inputs it requires, what outputs it produces. This white-box code analysis is sound because the implementation is ground truth; it cannot lie about capabilities like unstructured documentation can. Refining tool descriptions by grounding them in actual implementation ensures descriptions match behavior. Aggregating refined tool descriptions into server-level documentation creates a uniform retrieval target. This three-stage pipeline works because retrieval relies on having clear, complete, accurate descriptions; vague documentation causes retrieval failures. By extracting function truth from code rather than relying on human-written docs, the system guarantees retrieval works on both explicit and implicit function searches. Benchmarking on real-world server retrieval validates that white-box extraction genuinely improves selection accuracy compared to reading scattered original documentation.
